articles.title: HOW PAUL PRESENTS HIMSELF TO THE CORINTHIANS
articles.author: J. Renton

paragraphs.text: 1 Corinthians 3: 9–11; 4: 14–17; 7: 40; 9: 19; 15: These verses indicate some of the ways in which Paul presented himself to the Corinthians. He was known to the saints in Corinth, and they were known to him, because he had lived there for eighteen months. His presentation of himself would therefore be supported by what the Corinthians knew Paul to be. He presents himself in a way that would help the Corinthians. The Corinthians needed adjustment, help, and instruction, just as in our localities there is similar need. Although Paul was an apostle, some features in which he presents himself in this epistle could in some measure be taken on by us in our localities.

In chapter 1 Paul presents himself as an apostle . He says, “Paul, a called apostle of Jesus Christ, by God’s will” (1 Corinthians 1: 1), which would be unique to Paul. He had official authority as an apostle. That would not obtain today, but he also presents himself in other features which in measure, I believe, could be taken on by us.

In chapter 3 he presents himself as a wise architect which would be special to Paul too, but it would be a good question to ask ourselves what is the and in view in our activities, our desires, and our prayers in our localities. Paul’s activities in Corinth were governed by the light

that he had as an architect. He could see what God had in mind in that locality. He had the view of God’s building, for His pleasure, in which God could dwell. Paul refers to a shrine, a temple, where God’s presence would be known, where light would shine and God’s mind would be known. Paul as the wise architect had all this in mind when he preached and taught in Corinth. He says, “We are God’s fellow-workmen”. He and those with him worked together in view of arriving at God’s objective in that locality. It is a great matter, dear brethren, to have God’s objective in any activity we undertake. Paul laid the foundation in keeping with his understanding as an architect. What he laid was the foundation, but the foundation conformed to the structure that the architect had in mind. He says here, “According to the grace of God which has been given to me, as a wise architect, I have laid the foundation, but another builds upon it”.

He exhorts others to build according to that foundation. The foundation was laid with the architect’s view of the building in mind; they were to conform to the foundation which was laid there. “I have laid the foundation, but another builds upon it. But let each see how he builds upon it. For other foundation can no man lay besides that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ”. It is another order of Man that Paul laid as the foundation at Corinth, Jesus Christ. He tells us earlier in the epistle “And I, when I came to you, brethren, came not in excellency of word, or wisdom, announcing to you the testimony of God. For I did not judge it well to know anything among you save Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2: 1, 2). He had in mind to lay the foundation in Corinth in accord with another order of Man. That is what our local assemblies are to be. They are to be

conformed to another kind of Man, Jesus Christ. Nothing of the first man, and nothing of the man after the flesh was to enter into this structure that Paul had in mind as a wise architect, and therefore he laid the foundation.

Others were building upon it and they were not all building in keeping with the foundation. We need therefore to be watchful in our localities. How important it is to have a right objective in all our activities locally, in measure the objective Paul had in his labours in Corinth. He would discount every other man, no matter how eloquent, no matter what personal appeal they might have in human wisdom or that kind of thing. Paul laid the foundation, which is Jesus Christ, and he exhorts others to build according to the foundation he had laid. How important, therefore, to have some idea of what we are working for, what we are praying for, and the end to which we are labouring. Paul had this objective at Corinth as a wise architect. Everything was to conform to God’s own thought, God’s pleasure in another Man, Jesus Christ.

In the tabernacle of old the boards were of acacia wood. They were of the same kind of wood as the ark. That was the structure that supported the curtains in the tabernacle of which Moses was the architect as Paul was the architect at Corinth. It is all in view of another kind of Man, Jesus Christ. Let us judge every feature of the first man and of the man after the flesh so that we are building according to the foundation.

Now in chapter 4 Paul presents himself as a father. He says, “I think that God has set us the apostles for the last, as appointed to death. For we have become a spectacle to the world, both to angels and men” (1 Corinthians 4: 9). The fact is that the

Corinthians’ father, Paul, was under reproach and suffering and the Corinthians were not faithful children of their father. They were considering for themselves. Paul says, “Already ye are filled; already ye have been enriched; ye have reigned without us; and I would that ye reigned, that we also might reign with you” (1 Corinthians 4: 8). “We are fools for Christ’s sake, but ye prudent in Christ—we weak, but ye strong—ye glorious, but we in dishonour” (1 Corinthians 4: 10). Paul and Sosthenes were persecuted and insulted, while the Corinthians were enriched and were reigning; they were not true children of their father. So he says to them, “Not as chiding do I write these things to you, but as my beloved children I admonish you”.

What a powerful appeal he made to these Corinthians! Their behaviour was not in keeping with the conduct of their father. We often quote this scripture, “Yet not many fathers”, and that would be true that there are not many fathers. The fact is that the Corinthians had one father, Paul. He says, “For if ye should have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet not many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the glad tidings”. He had the right to claim them as his children, being an apostle. No one could claim today to be a father as Paul was, but there is plenty of room for fatherly affections, fatherly influence, and fatherly appeal to young people and to the saints locally and generally. The feelings and affections of a father are needed. What a powerful appeal this would make to the Corinthians and, to complete it, he sent Timotheus. He said to the Corinthians, “Not as chiding do I write these things to you, but as my beloved children I admonish you”, but he says regarding Timotheus, “For this reason I have sent to you Timotheus, who is my beloved and faithful child in

the Lord”. He could not say to the Corinthians, ‘You are my beloved and faithful children’, but he could say that in regard of Timotheus. Nevertheless, he appeals to them as, “My beloved children”. Even if they were not representing their father, even if they were not the faithful reproduction of their father, they certainly were beloved, and Paul’s fatherly affection came through and had its weight with these persons in Corinth. No one could have said, ‘Paul, you were not always like a father’. He had been eighteen months among them and he had been like a father. What they knew of him would support what he writes here.

Then he says, “I entreat you therefore, be my imitators”. Paul as a father represented in Corinth what all the saints should be. What a test that is!—to represent locally what the Lord intends all the saints should arrive at. That is what Paul represents. It is a very, very testing matter, but not an impossible one. In fact there would be some shortcoming in our prayers for our local brethren if the one who prayed did not somewhat represent what he was praying about for others. Paul represented what God intended all the saints in Corinth to arrive at, and he represented it in fatherly affection and fatherly influence, “I entreat you therefore, be my imitators”. Then he sent to them Timotheus, one who was his imitator, one who was his beloved and faithful child, showing that it is not impossible to be a faithful representation of Paul, to have Paul’s outlook, and feelings and affections. Paul’s appeal was reinforced by the presence amongst them of Timothy. The saints would look at Timothy and say, ‘He is a faithful representation of Paul himself. We had forgotten what Paul was like, but here he is, represented in this young man’. So a young man can take up this attitude that Timothy had here in

representing fatherly features. We have to learn to be sons before we can be fathers. We have to learn to be children before we can be parents, and Timothy no doubt learned to be a child of Paul and therefore could faithfully represent him.

Now in chapter 7 Paul presents himself as one who has God’s Spirit. You might say that every believer normally has the Spirit of God, and that would be true, but Paul says here, “I think that I also have God’s Spirit”. Not only had he received the Holy Spirit of God, but he had been formed by God’s Spirit. This chapter deals largely with the matter of marriage, but apart from what it deals with it is interesting to take note of how Paul speaks about himself. He says, for instance, in 1 Corinthians 7: 10, “But to the married I enjoin, not I, but the Lord”; that is, he emphasizes what is the Lord’s commandment, what it is obligatory on the part of every one to be subject to. Then he says in verse 12, “But as to the rest, I say, not the Lord”; that is, he goes on to speak of what he could not say specifically was the Lord’s commandment, but what he said. No doubt, as having God’s Spirit, he was qualified to say certain things.

It is good to accept direction from persons who have God’s Spirit. As having God’s Spirit, Paul’s judgment is reliable. He says, “According to my judgment; but I think that I also have God’s Spirit”; it is his judgment as having God’s Spirit. So he could say, “I say, not the Lord”. He could not exactly say, ‘This is a matter which is the Lord’s commandment and is obligatory and laid upon you to answer to. Who in Corinth or elsewhere would disregard what Paul said? Who in our localities would disregard what one who has God’s Spirit says is his judgment?—How important this is. We find salvation in the area

where persons who have God’s Spirit would give their judgment. Not that anyone is to be absolutely trusted; only the Lord is, and the Lord’s commandment is obligatory. Nevertheless, Paul says, “I say, not the Lord”. There are many references of this kind in this chapter.

Paul says in verse 25, “I give my opinion”. He gives his opinion as one who has God’s Spirit. He was a spiritual man. If we have such persons amongst us—and we speak to young people here, as well as older ones—we do well to listen to them. We might be saved many a sorrow if we listened to persons who would give their opinion as having God’s Spirit. What a desirable objective it would be on the part of every one of us to have God’s Spirit characteristically. It would come through giving place to the Spirit of God, being formed by the Spirit of God, so that we have the judgment God would have without being told directly what God’s judgment is.

The Lord’s commandment is specific and obligatory, but then there is the Lord’s mind. I have no doubt that “My opinion”, as Paul said, would be the Lord’s mind, and so he says in the last verse, “According to my judgment”—the judgment of one who has God’s Spirit.

In John 14 the Lord speaks about His commandments, “He that has my commandments and keeps them, he it is that loves me” (John 14: 21), and then He goes on to speak about “My word”, “If any one love me, he will keep my word “(verse 23). Then He speaks about “My words” (verse 24). Now the Lord’s commandment would be “Not I, but the Lord”, but then His mind would come in through persons who have God’s Spirit. We need to recognise where persons who have God’s Spirit would give their opinion, their

judgment. We would find salvation, beloved brethren, in listening and being subject to such persons. Therefore Paul presents himself to the Corinthians as having God’s Spirit. Besides his apostleship and the authority that he had, there is what the man was morally, formed morally as having God’s Spirit. What room there is in our localities for persons who have God’s Spirit! What an objective it should be on the part of every one of us to be formed in God’s Spirit, because matters come up where judgment is needed, where opinions need to be expressed. How important that those who express their opinion, or give their judgment, should have God’s Spirit.

In chapter 9 Paul presents himself as being free from all. He was under obligation to no one. He had no special friends, he had no party affiliations, nothing of that kind. He was free from all. His obligation was to his Lord and Master. He tells us (1 Corinthians 9: 9) that even the ox that trod the corn had certain rights; even the plougher had certain rights, but he says in verse 15, “I have used none of these things”. He had served at Corinth, and was serving them now in this letter, under obligation to no one. “Being free from all, I have made myself bondman to all”. What a man he was! What an influence he had! This is what the man was morally. He had only one loyalty and that was to the Lord Jesus, his Master. How important that each one of us should be like this! You can scarcely lift a volume of Mr. Taylor’s ministry without there being some reference in it to the dangers of partisanship and special friendships. That dear servant laboured at this matter. He could see the danger.
Paul was free from all, under obligation to

no one. He did not look for credit, nor did he look for approval. He did not look for any personal advantage; nothing of that kind marked the labours of Paul in Corinth and elsewhere. Thus, as looking for nothing in return, he was free from all in order to be more fully available as the bondman of all. “For being free from all, I have made myself bondman to all, that I might gain the most possible”. Oh how large was Paul’s outlook! We need to have our outlook enlarged that we might gain the most possible. I am calling attention to these features in which Paul presents himself to the Corinthians, and his presentation in his letter would be supported by what they knew the man to be. Alas, very few of us have been consistent. Paul was, and his consistency no doubt would have weight in the letter he wrote. How inconsistent we have been! How we departed, to our shame, from what we were brought to know as the truth! Even so, we can repent of all our diversions, of all our failures; we can repent of all, and as we thoroughly repent we can be morally clear. Where there has been failure and repentance the Lord can take account of what a man has been in the main objective of his life; but Paul had not deviated. Paul was consistent; “Being free from all, I have made myself bondman to all”. He was more completely a bondman to all because he was free from all, under no influence and no obligation, and at no personal advantage.

Now in the last scripture we read Paul appeals to the Corinthians as a brother. He says, “So then, my beloved brethren”. We use this expression, “Beloved brethren”, somewhat frequently in addressing the saints, but Paul uses this language very sparingly. He wrote to the Philippians, “My brethren, beloved and longed for, my joy and crown” (Philippians 4: 1), but apart from that I do not know of

anywhere else where Paul says, “My beloved brethren”. He appeals as a brother, and how important that is in our links together as brethren, including, of course, sisters. There will come a day when the wise architect will be no longer needed, and being bondman to all will no longer be needed; but the brother will go through into eternity. It belongs to the divine family. So Paul says, “my beloved brethren”. He had said in 1 Corinthians 4, “My beloved children”. That is a father. That too will cease—Paul will not be a father in eternity, but he will be a brother. He says, “So then, my beloved brethren, be firm, immovable, abounding always in the work of the Lord, knowing that your toil is not in vain in the Lord”. It comes at the end of a great opening up of teaching. Paul wrote in chapter 1, “But of him” (that is, God) “are ye in in Christ Jesus, who has been made to us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and holiness” (or sanctification) “and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1: 30). He has gone over all this ground in this epistle, and after concluding with the great matter of redemption, including resurrection, he says, “So then, my beloved brethren”, 1 Corinthians 15: 58. He is alongside of these persons in Corinth as one of them. He says, “Be firm, immovable, abounding always”. They can have confidence that the work of the Lord is going to go through. The very teaching of resurrection would show that everything is going through. “Abounding always”—not only abounding, but “abounding always in the work of the Lord, knowing that your toil is not in vain in the Lord”.

I believe that these ways in which Paul presents himself to the Corinthians can be in measure taken on by each one of us so that a right influence is brought to bear locally and that conditions may improve for the glory and pleasure of God. May it be so for His name’s sake.

Despite the increasing darkness of the day in which we live and the evident encroachment of the apostasy, the public testimony of God as to the glad tidings is still very pronounced in the way of preachings, in the giving away of tracts, and many other ways—even the board outside a meeting room—in which there is a public testimony to men and women that God is continuing the day of grace. These things make some impact upon the minds of men and women. I am quite sure that many of them say to themselves, ‘What has Christ got to offer me? What can He offer me more than I have just now?’.

Beloved hearers, I would like to speak tonight of some of the great blessings that God has to offer you in the glad tidings. Not that I could compass all the blessings—to do so would be impossible. All the blessings that God would offer to men in the glad tidings are so great, are so widespread, are so far-reaching, that I can only be selective in what I have to speak of.

I want to speak of three great spheres of blessing into which God would bring men in the acceptance of the glad tidings. That is something which should appeal to every man and woman because there is so little blessing in this world. Even circumstantially men’s lives these days are over-clouded by shadows,

sorrows, and calamities of every kind, so that it is good news to speak of blessing to men and to call their attention to great spheres of blessing which they can come into through the glad tidings. These scriptures that we have read show us that we may have access into these places of blessing. I suppose there is no more frustrating experience, even for the boys, than to see the sign, ‘No access’. You go this way—‘No access’; another way—‘No access’. But you never find that in the gospel. God in the glad tidings is opening the door to every sphere of blessing for men so that they may come into it tonight. Even the youngest may come into it— enter in in all your guilt and need and find a Saviour. The hymn says—
‘Christ is the Saviour of sinners,
Christ is the Saviour for me’.

Has everybody in this room really sung that in their hearts, that Christ is the Saviour for me? He offers me blessing; He offers through His own precious, finished work access into the great blessings that God has in His heart for men tonight. So this woman had access to the feet of Jesus. In that house of Simon the Pharisee, God saw to it that that woman in her burden and in her need would find access to that place where the blessed Saviour was ready to administer the forgiveness of sins to a poor and needy heart. What a sphere of blessing! That woman had never known this in her life before. She had known sorrow, she had known what it was to taste the wells of bitterness of this world, but in that house of Simon the Pharisee—in the most unlikely environment—she found access to a place of blessing for the forgiveness of her sins.
Have you ever found that place? Have you ever searched for it? Have you ever been affected by the Spirit of God in the preaching of the glad

tidings—so that you have longed to find that place of blessing, that initial place of blessing where Jesus speaks these feeling words, “Thy sins are forgiven”? Here was this woman, with the burdens that were in her heart, and she sought out that only place—think of that, that only place in the whole world—where she could have that wondrous message of forgiveness. She sought it out and was prepared to brave even the hardness and the coldness of that religious Pharisee in order to find a place of blessing. Oh how earnest she was! If there is one thing, beloved hearers, I would love to see, it is persons in earnest about the matter of their links with Christ and their links with God—in earnest about it, feeling that the issues of life and death and what is eternal are pressing upon them, and that they must be in earnest about it. This woman was really in earnest. She sought out the feet of Jesus and she expressed her appreciation of that wonderful pathway that opened up before her as it had never done before—the wonderful sphere of blessing for her heart.
Oh what a day it was! She could sing, ‘O happy day that fixed my choice’,
‘Happy day, when Jesus washed my sins away.
He teaches me to watch and pray
And live rejoicing every day.
Happy day! Happy day!’

Is that not wonderful? That woman was like that. She had reached a sphere of blessing. She had tasted wells of bitterness, wells of anguish, but that day as she went into that house she found access to the most blessed spot on earth, the feet of Jesus. She would sing that hymn— she would sing its equivalent—she would be touched in her heart that at last she had found a place where instead of judgment, instead of sorrow, blessing was being administered. How her ears must have

been touched to hear these words from Jesus, “Thy sins are forgiven”. Have you ever had a touch like that from the Lord—‘Thy sins are forgiven thee’? How essential it is to have soul dealings with Christ!

I am convinced, if I may say so, that any lack of fervency in meetings is because links with the Lord in regard of these blessed transactions have never been fully experienced. There is such a thing as ‘being converted’. I am not saying that everybody should be able to give the date and the hour and the place when they were converted—not everybody is able to do that. But I do believe this, that there is an experience in which you hear the Lord’s own voice, experience His own touch, and He says to you in His own words, ‘Thy sins are forgiven thee’. That provides a wondrous basis from which you grow in love and affection for Jesus.

It says, “And they that were with them at table began to say within themselves, Who is this who forgives also sins? And he said to the woman, Thy faith has saved thee; go in peace”. You know, there are thousands of souls in this world tonight searching for the message that the Lord gave this woman. They are trying every means possible to get it, they are searching every possible source to get peace, and they can find it only at the feet of Jesus.

Oh, if men and women would only come to that, that God has a Man in whose hand there is the solution, not only of every problem in the universe, but to every problem in the life and history of each man, and woman, and boy and girl. There is a Man who has the answer to it— “Go in peace”. Have you heard these words? If so,
amidst all the burden of things in this scene you know that, because you have settled that great matter of your link with Christ, you can go in peace.

In Romans 5 you find another wondrous sphere of blessing; “Therefore having been justified on the principle of faith, we have peace towards God through our Lord Jesus Christ”. What a sphere of blessing! Perhaps we do not hear as much as we should in the preaching about justification, because there is a lot of unhappiness with some, a lot of doubts sometimes, a lot of anxiety as to whether their links with the Lord Jesus are really permanent. I find that if you speak with men and women at large many will say, ‘Well, yes, I know that Jesus died for me, but I have just a doubt in my mind as to whether, when it comes to the final reckoning, I shall be saved’. Well, how thankful we are for the truth of justification by faith. You know, there are thousands of souls in a not very wide radius from here who are enslaved in a system of darkness, who believe with absolute confidence that the answer to the peace of their souls lies in what they can bring, and what they can give, to a hierarchical system.

Now here is a blessed Man, the Lord Jesus Christ, and God looks at you in all the perfection and blessedness of His finished work. As God sees that Man, risen from the dead in all His acceptance in His presence, God looks at every believer and there will never be a sin, never a charge, never an imputation of guilt, against any person who trusts in our Lord Jesus Christ. Are you troubled? Despite the fact that you once committed yourself to the Lord, do you have an uneasy feeling sometimes? Do you wake up in the night and say, ‘Am I really saved?’. Does the enemy get at you and say, ‘Well, you did something

yesterday, you allowed something to happen yesterday—How are you going to be a christian if that happened?’. We have all had these experiences. How wonderful just to get your eye on a Man in the presence of God in all His glory. His finished work accepted up there, and God’s eye resting complacently on Him.

There never was a day like the present in which there is a new religious cult coming into prominence almost every week. New cults are springing up because men and women are seeking satisfaction for their souls. Anybody who can produce something that tends even for a moment to allay soul hunger gets a hearing. What does that speak of? It speaks of the longing that men and women have for something that will satisfy their souls amidst all the materialism and empty pleasures of this world. I can tell you this with certainty, that none of these so-called ‘faiths’ can present as glad tidings a living glorious Man in the presence of God, who is the standard of your acceptance, the measure of your forgiveness, the surety of your joy, and the extent of your privilege. None of them can offer that. The only Person who can provide an answer to the need of your soul is Jesus in the presence of God. Hallelujah! What a Saviour! How wonderful!

It says, “Having been justified on the principle of faith, we have peace towards God through our Lord Jesus Christ; by whom we have also access by faith into this favour in which we stand”. We have favour, and access into the highest circles. Nothing is barred, the highest circles of privilege, the highest circles of acceptance, and “we boast in hope of the glory of God”. Men are very boastful these days, are they not? The arrogance of men makes one tremble sometimes—the utterly profane way in which they speak of God and of Christ. Yet here is something that we can boast in—“We boast in hope of the glory of God”. God is going to fill this world with all that He has found in that beloved Man. He will fill it with the glory of that Man who is rejected at the present time. What a thought that is! At the Supper this morning Ecclesiastes 10: 7 was quoted, “I have seen servants upon horses, and princes walking as servants upon the earth”, emphasising the place of reproach of the believer consequent on the rejection of the Lord Jesus. That is what happens today; but the day is coming when God will manifest the glory of His beloved Son and the servants will be walking on the earth and the princes will be riding on horseback. What a change! “We boast in hope of the glory of God”. Dear young people, I would appeal to you. I do not think, despite all the sorrow that has come into things publicly, that there is anything greater to which a person can devote his or her life than the testimony of God. Despite what has been incurred in the way of reproach and condemnation in the eyes of men, this remains, that the testimony of God regarding Christ, carried in faith and affection at the present time, is the greatest matter to which persons can devote themselves.

Dear young people, do not let the opportunities of this world divert you from that. You may say, ‘Well, it is all right for you, an old person, you have had your day, you have had your run of things in this world’. Do not let that divert you; but in your own simple way commit yourself to the testimony of God.

In Ephesians we find another sphere of blessing: “For through him we have both access by one Spirit to the Father”. What a place of blessing! I do not think anybody will question me about bringing this into the preaching. I do not think anybody will say,

‘That is not part of the glad tidings’. Of course it is! It is part of the blessing in the glad tidings that we have access to the Father. How wonderful are the privileges of christianity! Christianity is essentially a system of privilege. It carries its responsibilities. Once you confess the name of the Lord Jesus the responsibilities that devolve upon you are immense— so are the resources in the Holy Spirit to enable you to meet them. But essentially christianity is a system of privilege. Now here is the greatest privilege that anyone could have, “access by one Spirit to the Father”. “So then ye are no longer strangers and foreigners, but ye are fellow-citizens of the saints, and of the household of God”.

I like that word, “the household of God”. I think everybody will know the difference between a house and a household. The house is where order is maintained. A man is head of his house and maintains order there. But the household is a sphere of the administration of blessing, and it says here that we are “of the household of God”. Oh the blessings that God dispenses in His household! We have enjoyed some of them these past three days. That has distinctly impressed me, the household of God, and God not only maintaining order in His house, not only saying that these are the standards that have to be maintained (as befits God, things must be such as please Him), but God in His household administering food and blessing, care and comfort. What a household to be in!

Beloved brother, is your household like that? Do the children feel like that? Do they say, This is not only a house, but a household, where there is an administration of blessing, joy, and peace. That is something that brings the impress of heaven into the lives of the young people, that takes away

the spirit of legality and replaces it by the features of a household, the household of faith, the household of God. How would God conduct His household? He conducts it in a beneficent way and ministers blessing to men. It says, “Being built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the corner-stone”. What a house! What a sphere of privilege to see one glorious Man as the corner-stone of that dwelling. You look round at the edifices of this world. Think of a young man going down to Westminster, seeing the Houses of Parliament, or up in our part of the world seeing Holyrood Palace, and he would say, ‘No, they are none of them like where I belong. None of them has a corner-stone like this—“Jesus Christ himself being the corner-stone”. It is the thought of beautification; it imparts a feeling of dignity. O, beloved hearers, christians are to be dignified persons. You do not go through this world grovelling, just giving people an impression that you have to be very apologetic if you speak about the Lord. No, no! a christian is marked by dignity because Jesus Christ Himself is the chief corner-stone of that wonderful edifice and you find yourself a part of it.

It says, “In whom all the building fitted together increases to a holy temple in the Lord; in whom ye also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit”. What a sphere of blessing!—to find constantly that your soul is being brightened and watered and strengthened. There is an area of things down here in this world, and we must call attention to it. I was thankful that our brother today made an appeal in regard to the breaking of bread in his preaching. When I was a young person there was rarely a preaching that did not include an appeal to the young people to commit themselves to the Lord in the breaking of

bread. But what are they committing themselves to? Are they committing themselves only to a position of reproach? No; they are committing themselves to a great sphere of blessing, growing up as constantly supplied by the river of God, constantly supplied by divine provision, and growing up to something that is going to be for the pleasure of God Himself, in which He will dwell. That is christianity. What has Christ to offer me? Heaven when I die? Just that? Is that all Christ has to offer me? No—He will give you now the forgiveness of your sins, access into this favour in which we stand, and access into the presence of the Father, now! I know there are anticipative thoughts in christianity; the Scriptures are full of what is anticipative; but the glory of the present moment is what, in the Spirit’s power, can be experienced an enjoyed now. May we all come into it, for His name’s sake.

2 Corinthians 6: 9 (first part); Hebrews 11: 35–I wondered, dear brethren, if the Lord would say something to us as to our going on in faith with no seen result, but with the consciousness that we are known of Him. This last section in Hebrews 11 is somewhat impersonal. Up to verse 34 it is largely the great triumphs of faith, including what was seen outwardly, even, as it says, to overcoming kingdoms and making armies give way. But this latter section that we have read is impersonal;

there are no names mentioned. That raises the question with us all as to whether we are prepared to go on unrecognised, unknown. One is always touched when passing a war memorial. Usually certain names are inscribed, but there are unknown persons who were in the same category, unknown and unsung, and what they did was as great in its way as the deeds of those who are named.

I ask myself whether one is prepared to go on unknown, even in a certain sense among the brethren (you understand what I mean), quietly going on not seeking prominence, not making any noise, but just going on. It is important, I think, that in some way we each face this matter of preparedness to go on with no seen result, but carrying in one’s soul and affections and consciousness the sense of the Lord’s approval—“unknown, and well known”.

It is not the only outlook that we are to have, of course, for there is the side of company. I think that is contained in this reference, “They went about in sheepskins”. Sheep are found in flocks. This probably relates also to the suffering character of the pathway—“As a sheep dumb before her shearers” (Isaiah 53: 7)—what a model He has left us! So part of their experience was that they went about in sheepskins. It was a suffering path, but they found company in it. We are not to be without this experience of having company and fellowship, which in a right sense is of God, and is a great support, encouragement, and source of strengthening. Even seeing the faces of one another is a cheer—face brightens face.
But it also says that they went about in goatskins, as if that was a concurrent experience (and an important one, I think). I say this as feeling in some way the need for it myself, to be

prepared to go about, so to speak, in a goatskin. I know that Scripture speaks about the flock of goats, but generally the goat is a separate animal. It is an individual, so to speak, having periods of apparent loneliness, but never out of God’s all-seeing eye. There it is, solitary maybe—not like a flock of sheep on the hills pasturing themselves—but just a single goat. The goat seems able to sustain such a life.

Now one would not like to divorce these two aspects, “They went about in sheepskins, in goatskins”. You might say, one day a sheepskin, another day a goatskin, both experiences going on together; experiences with one another in the company, and experiences individually; and that, dear brethren, was especially on one’s mind just now, that every one of us should know what it is to be “unknown, and well known”, and should covet a sense of the Lord’s approval—His own direct approval. The Lord knew all the disciples. He said, “Ye are they who have persevered with me in my temptations” (Luke 22: 28); but He also knew each one. Doubtless he observed and considered and assessed each one. Have you a sense that the Lord knows you, that you are well known? Do you covet that sense, do you cherish it? It is a great thing, dear brethren, in the joy of our occasions together, to maintain our own sense that the Lord knows us and we are known of Him; that will see you through when you are alone.
I recently came across some words of Columba, written in the sixth century—
‘Alone, with none but Thee, O God,
I journey on my way ...’.
I could not but be impressed with that. He lived in a different time, but to write those words he must have had a sense of what is was to be just
conscious of being with God. He was used to bring the gospel to these islands, but what I want to stress is that he had some impression of being alone with God, and moving under His eye.

So in this section of the Scriptures the apostle has spoken about names which are repeated time and time again in the holy writings—Abraham, Jacob. Moses, and others—we might say names of fame, and rightly so. Then the Spirit of God goes over the unknown ones. He does not miss them. Dear brethren, I ask again, Am I prepared to be unknown, just go on day by day in my lot, maybe in an obscure place, but seen by God Himself, and recorded and known in heaven? These persons had no miraculous outward deliverance, they were tortured, tempted, and tried, but they are placed in, we might say, heaven’s roll of honour and are known up there. It is a secret, dear brethren, that one would like to carry and cherish, not to live in externals, but to live in the sense of having the Lord’s approval—“unknown, and well known”.

Here we are; we are not taken account of publicly. Alas, there are sorrows we have added to the public position, but none of us has a name in public christendom. And if you wanted it, (I trust not one of us does), the most you could hope for is a name in a comparatively small circle. It is not worth it! The thing is to be known in heaven.

Hence I would just encourage us all to maintain this feature of going about in a goatskin; but, do not forget, there is also a sheepskin. We are not seeking to set one thing over against another; these things are to coalesce in our experience, they are to go along together.

Companionship is a very fine experience in which we find comfort. It is normal for a believer to find joy and comfort in it—“And having been let go, they came to their own company” (Acts 4: 23); “let go”, it is like the bowstring released and springing back to its normal place.

So these persons went about in sheepskins—in fact, that is put first, as if it is the normal thing; yet it must be, may I say simply, supported by the goatskins, otherwise you may (to employ an expression which we often use) just live on the meetings, which is not right. We should maintain and cherish this idea of the covering of goatskin. I know it involves separation on the one side, but I am just speaking of it more as what is individual.

So the believer goes on, day after day, unknown, unlettered, and unsung; but he goes on. Day after day, and no one appears to notice him, but he is known in heaven. You can understand such a believer, when he is raptured, not being missed, can you not? You can understand such a person going on quietly, steadily, patiently—the day of the rapture will come—he will be gone! What will his neighbours say? They can give no account of him; he was unknown. They will say, There was always a certain mystery about him. It is like Enoch—men could give no account of him; he was translated. He was unknown, I suppose, among his contemporaries, he had no name in their circle, but he was well known elsewhere. How well known he was! So he was raptured, he was taken; men could give no account of him. That would be normal, dear brethren. I wonder if it will be so with me. There will be believers, perhaps, like Lot, who will be taken from situations which are not really compatible with their heavenly calling. That is the abnormal side, but, viewed normally,
the saints will go, and men will be unable to give an account of them—unknown, and yet well known.

Well, that is all that I had to say, dear brethren, that we might maintain carefully, and not give up, either the sheepskin or the goatskin. They are both important. The former is perhaps more visible than the other, it is more apparent, involving some measure of mutual testimony, but we must also maintain this more individual idea of the goatskin. Paul says he went on “unknown, and well known”. He and those with him were going on in that way. May the Lord encourage us in these things, for His name’s sake.

God intends to display the surpassing riches of His grace in kindness towards us in Christ Jesus (Ephesians 2: 7). This will be seen in persons such as ourselves. We are His treasures and He will delight to display them so that others can enter into His joy and see what is in His heart. He does not display His judgment but His grace. Men with collections of precious objects find pleasure in displaying them and sharing their joys with others. How much more so the blessed God! We shall be His in the day that He prepares (Malachi 3: 17); we are His workmanship in Christ Jesus. The Spirit’s demonstration is now, but the display is in the coming ages in glory.
Kingston, Ont.

THE DOORKEEPERS’ TRUST In 1 Chronicles 9 we are told the services which were entrusted to the doorkeepers. These services were by no means limited to controlling entrance to the house, though surely the doorkeepers would impart a sense of welcome to those who approached suitably, as well as ensuring that no one unsuitable entered the house. But they had a privileged responsibility much wider than that. They opened the house every morning, and under their charge were the treasuries of the house, and the instruments of service, which they brought in by number. They were also over the vessels, the holy instruments, the fine flour, the wine, the oil, the frankincense, and the spices. Each morning as they opened the house all would therefore be in readiness for the service to begin, with its holy instruments, the fresh appreciation of Christ typified in the fine flour, the holy stimulation for God suggested in the wine, the fresh flow of the Holy Spirit indicated in the oil, and what speaks of the fragrance of Christ resting upon the saints. It is also said that the doorkeepers “stayed round about the house of God during the night”.

Let us, by the Spirit, commit ourselves to this charge so as to ensure the constant maintenance of what is delightful to God. Thus, as the saints assemble, all would be in order and readiness for the service (whatever its character) to proceed in the liberty, harmony, fulness, and fragrance suited to the house, and so delightful to Him who dwells in it.

The Lord is not quick to discard us, you know. He is very patient with us. He holds on to us. There is no idea that these men lost their apostleship in the fact that they went off fishing. There is no thought that Peter lost his apostleship, because he denied the Lord. There is not a word about that. The Lord never brings it up. I am speaking thus that we might come to regard the Lord even in the service. He does not discard us quickly. He values us and He never forgets our best moments, what we used to be; in our darkest moments the Lord never forgets the brightest moment.

I remember well a sister saying to me once, she had been in a storm at sea, and at the time she was thinking of Jesus asleep in the storm. I said, That is not the way to look at Jesus. If you had been looking at Him where He is, He would have made you like what He was in the storm. You must get your connection with Jesus where He is. How do I get skill to be as Jesus was here? Let me give you one single statement to keep definitely in your souls. You must see Him where He is, to be like Him where He was. You must see Him where He is; not be looking at Him where He was.
